items.stem: Why is `unknown` often safer than `any` for an untyped value?

options.text: unknown forces you to narrow before use, while any disables type checking
options.rationale: Correct: unknown preserves type safety by requiring a check; any opts out entirely.

options.text: unknown is faster at run time
options.rationale: Types are erased at run time; there is no speed difference.

options.text: any cannot be assigned to variables
options.rationale: any can be assigned freely; that is the problem.

options.text: unknown allows any method call directly
options.rationale: unknown blocks direct member access until narrowed.

items.explanation: Correct: unknown preserves type safety by requiring a check; any opts out entirely.

items.stem: Which TWO are good reasons to use a discriminated union? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The compiler can narrow by the discriminant property
options.rationale: Correct: a literal discriminant enables precise narrowing.

options.text: It enables exhaustiveness checks with never
options.rationale: Correct: an unhandled case surfaces as a never error.

options.text: It removes the need for any types
options.rationale: Avoiding any is good practice generally, not the purpose of a discriminated union.

options.text: It makes casting with as safe
options.rationale: Discriminated unions reduce the need to cast, not make casts safe.

items.explanation: Correct: a literal discriminant enables precise narrowing.

items.stem: Enabling strict mode surfaces many 'possibly undefined' errors. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Fix the code to handle the undefined cases
options.rationale: Correct: strict null checks reveal real gaps that should be handled.

options.text: Disable strict to remove the errors
options.rationale: Disabling strict hides real bugs rather than fixing them.
Casting to any defeats the type system.
Blanket ignores suppress genuine type errors.

items.explanation: Correct: strict null checks reveal real gaps that should be handled.
